claim: The study analyzed data from 3521 women and men aged 60 years and older.
source: We analysed data obtained from 3521 women and men aged 60 years and older, whose fracture incidence, mortality, and bone mineral density (BMD) have been monitored since 1989.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sample size and age criteria in the abstract.

claim: Fracture incidence, mortality, and bone mineral density (BMD) have been monitored since 1989.
source: We analysed data obtained from 3521 women and men aged 60 years and older, whose fracture incidence, mortality, and bone mineral density (BMD) have been monitored since 1989.
evidence: The manuscript states the monitoring period and parameters in the abstract.

claim: During the 20-year follow-up period, 632 women and 184 men sustained a first incident fracture.
source: During the 20-year follow-up period, among 632 women and 184 men with a first incident fracture, the risk of sustaining a second fracture was higher in women (36%) than in men (22%), but mortality risk was higher in men (41%) than in women (25%).
evidence: The abstract provides specific numbers of participants with first incident fractures.

claim: The risk of sustaining a second fracture was higher in women (36%) than in men (22%).
source: During the 20-year follow-up period, among 632 women and 184 men with a first incident fracture, the risk of sustaining a second fracture was higher in women (36%) than in men (22%), but mortality risk was higher in men (41%) than in women (25%).
evidence: The abstract provides specific percentages for second fracture risk by gender.

claim: Mortality risk following a first incident fracture was higher in men (41%) than in women (25%).
source: During the 20-year follow-up period, among 632 women and 184 men with a first incident fracture, the risk of sustaining a second fracture was higher in women (36%) than in men (22%), but mortality risk was higher in men (41%) than in women (25%).
evidence: The abstract provides specific percentages for mortality risk by gender.

claim: The increased risk of mortality was not only present with an initial fracture, but was accelerated with refractures.
source: The increased risk of mortality was not only present with an initial fracture, but was accelerated with refractures.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the relationship between refractures and mortality risk.

claim: Male gender is a key predictor of post-fracture mortality with a hazard ratio of 2.4 (95% CI, 1.79–3.21).
source: Key predictors of post-fracture mortality were male gender (hazard ratio [HR] 2.4; 95% CI, 1.79–3.21), advancing age (HR 1.67; 1.53–1.83), and lower femoral neck BMD (HR 1.16; 1.01–1.33).
evidence: The abstract provides specific hazard ratio and confidence interval for male gender.

claim: Advancing age is a key predictor of post-fracture mortality with a hazard ratio of 1.67 (95% CI, 1.53–1.83).
source: Key predictors of post-fracture mortality were male gender (hazard ratio [HR] 2.4; 95% CI, 1.79–3.21), advancing age (HR 1.67; 1.53–1.83), and lower femoral neck BMD (HR 1.16; 1.01–1.33).
evidence: The abstract provides specific hazard ratio and confidence interval for advancing age.

claim: Lower femoral neck BMD is a key predictor of post-fracture mortality with a hazard ratio of 1.16 (95% CI, 1.01–1.33).
source: Key predictors of post-fracture mortality were male gender (hazard ratio [HR] 2.4; 95% CI, 1.79–3.21), advancing age (HR 1.67; 1.53–1.83), and lower femoral neck BMD (HR 1.16; 1.01–1.33).
evidence: The abstract provides specific hazard ratio and confidence interval for lower femoral neck BMD.

claim: A 70-year-old man with a fracture is predicted to have a skeletal age of 75.
source: A 70-year-old man with a fracture is predicted to have a skeletal age of 75.
evidence: The abstract provides a specific example of skeletal age calculation.

claim: From the age of 50, the residual lifetime risk of fracture is approximately 50% in women and approximately 30% in men.
source: From the age of 50, the residual lifetime risk of fracture is ~50% in women and ~30% in men (Nguyen et al., 2007a).
evidence: The introduction cites a previous study providing lifetime fracture risk estimates.

claim: In women, the lifetime risk of hip fracture is equivalent to or higher than the risk of invasive breast cancer.
source: In women, the lifetime risk of hip fracture is actually equivalent to or higher than the risk of invasive breast cancer (Nguyen et al., 2007a; Cummings et al., 1989).
evidence: The introduction cites previous studies comparing hip fracture risk to breast cancer risk.

claim: In men, the lifetime risk of hip and vertebral fractures (17%) is comparable to the lifetime risk of being diagnosed with prostate cancer.
source: In men, the lifetime risk of hip and vertebral fractures (17%) is comparable to the lifetime risk of being diagnosed with prostate cancer (Cummings et al., 1989; Shortt and Robinson, 2005).
evidence: The introduction cites previous studies comparing fracture risk to prostate cancer risk.

claim: In the United States, the cost attributable to osteoporosis and fracture was estimated to be $22 billion in 2008.
source: In the United States alone, the cost attributable to osteoporosis and fracture was estimated to be $22 billion (2008), higher than the cost attributable to breast cancer (Blume and Curtis, 2011).
evidence: The introduction cites a study providing cost estimates for osteoporosis and fracture.

claim: The cost attributable to osteoporosis and fracture in the United States is higher than the cost attributable to breast cancer.
source: In the United States alone, the cost attributable to osteoporosis and fracture was estimated to be $22 billion (2008), higher than the cost attributable to breast cancer (Blume and Curtis, 2011).
evidence: The introduction cites a study comparing costs of osteoporosis/fracture to breast cancer.

claim: An existing fracture signals an increased risk of subsequent fracture and/or mortality.
source: Various studies have found that an existing fracture signals an increased risk of subsequent fracture and/or mortality (Shortt and Robinson, 2005; Center et al., 2007; Bliuc et al., 2009).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple studies supporting this relationship.

claim: Existing fracture risk assessment tools focus on predicting the risk of an initial fracture but ignore the risks of refracture or mortality following an initial fracture.
source: Existing fracture risk assessment tools focus on predicting the risk of an initial fracture (Kanis et al., 2008; Nguyen et al., 2007b; Nguyen et al., 2008; Hippisley-Cox and Coupland, 2012), but ignore the risks of refracture or mortality following an initial fracture.
evidence: The introduction cites multiple risk assessment tools and identifies their limitation.

claim: The study included 2046 women and 1205 men, all aged 60 years and older at baseline.
source: The study included 2046 women and 1205 men, all aged 60 years and older at baseline.
evidence: The results section provides specific participant numbers by gender.

claim: Mean age at baseline was 70 (SD 7) in women and 70 (SD 6) in men.
source: Mean age at baseline was 70 (SD 7) in women and 70 (SD 6) in men.
evidence: The results section provides mean age and standard deviation by gender.

claim: At baseline, approximately 22% (n = 458) women and 9% (n = 111) men had osteoporosis (femoral neck BMD T-score ≤ –2.5).
source: At baseline, approximately 22% (n = 458) women and 9% (n = 111) men were having osteoporosis (femoral neck BMD T-score ≤ –2.5) (Table 1).
evidence: The results section and Table 1 provide osteoporosis prevalence data.

claim: Prior fracture (those occurring prior to study entry) was reported in 17.5% of women and 11.5% of men.
source: Prior fracture (those occurring prior to study entry) was reported in 17.5% of women and 11.5% of men.
evidence: The results section provides prior fracture prevalence by gender.

claim: More women (38%, n = 776) than men (26%, n = 317) self-reported a fall over the previous 12 months.
source: More women (38%, n = 776) than men (26%, n = 317) self-reported a fall over the previous 12 months.
evidence: The results section provides fall history data by gender.

claim: Men were more susceptible than women to cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.
source: Men were more susceptible than women to cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.
evidence: The results section states gender differences in comorbidities.

claim: On average, the first fracture occurred at age 79 (SD 8).
source: On average, the first fracture occurred at age 79 (SD 8), followed by the second fracture at age 82 (SD 7) and the third fracture at age 83 (SD 7; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The results section provides mean age at first fracture with reference to supplementary data.

claim: The second fracture occurred at age 82 (SD 7).
source: On average, the first fracture occurred at age 79 (SD 8), followed by the second fracture at age 82 (SD 7) and the third fracture at age 83 (SD 7; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The results section provides mean age at second fracture with reference to supplementary data.

claim: The third fracture occurred at age 83 (SD 7).
source: On average, the first fracture occurred at age 79 (SD 8), followed by the second fracture at age 82 (SD 7) and the third fracture at age 83 (SD 7; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The results section provides mean age at third fracture with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Age at death, including death following a fracture and death without a fracture, was 83 (SD 8).
source: Age at death, including death following a fracture and death without a fracture, was 83 (SD 8).
evidence: The results section provides mean age at death.

claim: Once a fracture occurred, men transitioned more quickly to adverse stages than women did.
source: Comparison between men and women reveals that despite the age at entry and at initial fracture was not substantially different, age at subsequent events, that is, second and third fracture and death, was younger in men than in women, suggesting that once a fracture occurred, men transitioned more quickly to adverse stages than women did (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The results section infers faster transition in men based on age at subsequent events.

claim: During the follow-up period, 632 (31%) women sustained at least one fracture over 21,723 person-years.
source: During the follow-up period, 632 (31%) women and 184 (15%) men who had sustained at least one fracture over 21,723 and 11,968 person-years were at risk, yielding a fracture incidence rate of 24 (95% CI, 22–26) and 15 (95% CI, 13–17) per 1000 person-years for women and men, respectively (Figure 1).
evidence: The results section and Figure 1 provide fracture incidence data for women.

claim: During the follow-up period, 184 (15%) men sustained at least one fracture over 11,968 person-years.
source: During the follow-up period, 632 (31%) women and 184 (15%) men who had sustained at least one fracture over 21,723 and 11,968 person-years were at risk, yielding a fracture incidence rate of 24 (95% CI, 22–26) and 15 (95% CI, 13–17) per 1000 person-years for women and men, respectively (Figure 1).
evidence: The results section and Figure 1 provide fracture incidence data for men.

claim: The fracture incidence rate was 24 (95% CI, 22–26) per 1000 person-years for women.
source: During the follow-up period, 632 (31%) women and 184 (15%) men who had sustained at least one fracture over 21,723 and 11,968 person-years were at risk, yielding a fracture incidence rate of 24 (95% CI, 22–26) and 15 (95% CI, 13–17) per 1000 person-years for women and men, respectively (Figure 1).
evidence: The results section and Figure 1 provide calculated fracture incidence rate for women.

claim: The fracture incidence rate was 15 (95% CI, 13–17) per 1000 person-years for men.
source: During the follow-up period, 632 (31%) women and 184 (15%) men who had sustained at least one fracture over 21,723 and 11,968 person-years were at risk, yielding a fracture incidence rate of 24 (95% CI, 22–26) and 15 (95% CI, 13–17) per 1000 person-years for women and men, respectively (Figure 1).
evidence: The results section and Figure 1 provide calculated fracture incidence rate for men.

claim: Among the 816 individuals with fracture, 270 went on to have another fracture, with 99 having more than two fractures.
source: Among the 816 individuals with fracture, 270 went on to have another fracture, with 99 having more than two fractures.
evidence: The results section provides data on subsequent fractures.

claim: 627 (31%) women died during the follow-up period, yielding a mortality rate of 33 (95% CI, 31–35) per 1000 person-years.
source: Overall, 627 (31%) women and 501 (42%) men had died over the same period, yielding a mortality rate of 33 (95% CI, 31–35) and 42 (95% CI, 38–46) per 1000 person-years for women and men, respectively.
evidence: The results section provides mortality data for women.

claim: 501 (42%) men died during the follow-up period, yielding a mortality rate of 42 (95% CI, 38–46) per 1000 person-years.
source: Overall, 627 (31%) women and 501 (42%) men had died over the same period, yielding a mortality rate of 33 (95% CI, 31–35) and 42 (95% CI, 38–46) per 1000 person-years for women and men, respectively.
evidence: The results section provides mortality data for men.

claim: Among the deceased, 262 (42%) women died following a fragility fracture.
source: Among the deceased, 262 (42%) women and 105 (57%) men died following a fragility fracture (Figure 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The results section and Figure 1 provide post-fracture mortality data for women.

claim: Among the deceased, 105 (57%) men died following a fragility fracture.
source: Among the deceased, 262 (42%) women and 105 (57%) men died following a fragility fracture (Figure 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The results section and Figure 1 provide post-fracture mortality data for men.

claim: In fracture-free women, the instantaneous risk of having the first fracture was 2.7% (95% CI, 2.4–3.0%).
source: In fracture-free women, the instantaneous risk of having the first fracture was 2.7% (95% CI, 2.4–3.0%).
evidence: The results section provides instantaneous risk data for first fracture in women.

claim: Once the initial fracture occurred in women, the risk of sustaining another fracture was almost doubled (4.8%; 95% CI, 3.8–6.3%).
source: Once the initial fracture occurred, the risk of sustaining another fracture was almost doubled (4.8%; 95% CI, 3.8–6.3%).
evidence: The results section provides instantaneous risk data for second fracture in women.

claim: Women with no fracture had the lowest risk of mortality (1.8%; 95% CI, 1.5–2.0%).
source: This trend was also observed for mortality: while women with no fracture had the lowest risk of mortality (1.8%; 95% CI, 1.5–2.0%), those with one, two, and three or more fractures had an increased risk of mortality from 2.1% to 12.9%.
evidence: The results section provides mortality risk data for fracture-free women.

claim: Women with one, two, and three or more fractures had an increased risk of mortality from 2.1% to 12.9%.
source: This trend was also observed for mortality: while women with no fracture had the lowest risk of mortality (1.8%; 95% CI, 1.5–2.0%), those with one, two, and three or more fractures had an increased risk of mortality from 2.1% to 12.9%.
evidence: The results section provides mortality risk data for women with fractures.

claim: The risk of first incident fracture was lower in men than in women (HR 0.63; 95% CI, 0.53–0.75).
source: The risk of first incident fracture was lower in men than in women (HR 0.63; 95% CI, 0.53–0.75).
evidence: The results section provides hazard ratio comparing first fracture risk between genders.

claim: There was no significant difference in the risk of second fracture between genders.
source: However, there was no significant difference in the risk of second fracture between genders.
evidence: The results section states lack of gender difference in second fracture risk.

claim: The risk of third fracture in men was 2.1-fold higher than that in women (HR 2.11; 95% CI, 1.13–3.95).
source: More interestingly, the risk of third fracture in men was 2.1-fold higher than that in women (HR 2.11; 95% CI, 1.13–3.95).
evidence: The results section provides hazard ratio comparing third fracture risk between genders.

claim: The risk of death, regardless of fracture status, was consistently higher in men than in women.
source: Moreover, the risk of death, regardless of fracture status, was consistently higher in men than in women (Table 2).
evidence: The results section and Table 2 show gender differences in mortality risk.

claim: Men were less likely than women to suffer an initial fracture (HR 0.63; 95% CI, 0.53–0.75).
source: As previously known, men were less likely than women to suffer an initial fracture (HR 0.63; 95% CI, 0.53–0.75), but after a fracture men were more likely than women to die (HR 2.40; 95% CI, 1.79–3.21) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The results section and Figure 2B provide hazard ratio for initial fracture by gender.

claim: After a fracture, men were more likely than women to die (HR 2.40; 95% CI, 1.79–3.21).
source: As previously known, men were less likely than women to suffer an initial fracture (HR 0.63; 95% CI, 0.53–0.75), but after a fracture men were more likely than women to die (HR 2.40; 95% CI, 1.79–3.21) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The results section and Figure 2B provide hazard ratio for post-fracture mortality by gender.

claim: In either men or women, advancing age was associated with an increased risk of initial fracture, second fracture, and mortality.
source: In either men or women, advancing age was associated with an increased risk of initial fracture, second fracture, and mortality.
evidence: The results section states the association between age and multiple outcomes.

claim: For a given age and gender, individuals with lower femoral neck BMD were associated with increased risks of initial fracture, second fracture, and mortality.
source: For a given age and gender, individuals with lower femoral neck BMD were associated with increased risks of initial fracture, second fracture, and mortality.
evidence: The results section states the association between BMD and multiple outcomes.

claim: A personal history of fracture was a risk factor for subsequent fracture, but was not associated with the transition between fracture and mortality.
source: A personal history of fracture was a risk factor for subsequent fracture, but was not associated with the transition between fracture and mortality.
evidence: The results section states the differential association of prior fracture with outcomes.

claim: In both women and men, those having rheumatoid arthritis were more likely to have an increased risk of initial fracture and second fracture.
source: In both women and men, those having rheumatoid arthritis were more likely to have an increased risk of initial fracture and second fracture (Figure 2A).
evidence: The results section and Figure 2A show the association between rheumatoid arthritis and fracture risk.

claim: Women tended to stay at each health state longer than men.
source: Women tended to stay at each health state longer than men.
evidence: The results section states gender differences in sojourn time.

claim: The predicted sojourn time in state 1 (fracture free) of a 'typical' woman with osteopenic BMD (T-score = −1.5) was 22.4 years.
source: The predicted sojourn time in state 1 (fracture free) of a 'typical' woman with osteopenic BMD (T-score = −1.5) was 22.4 years, 5.5 years longer than that of an osteoporotic woman (T-score = −2.5).
evidence: The results section provides specific sojourn time estimate for women with osteopenic BMD.

claim: The predicted sojourn time in state 1 (fracture free) of an osteoporotic woman (T-score = −2.5) was 5.5 years shorter than that of a woman with osteopenic BMD (T-score = −1.5).
source: The predicted sojourn time in state 1 (fracture free) of a 'typical' woman with osteopenic BMD (T-score = −1.5) was 22.4 years, 5.5 years longer than that of an osteoporotic woman (T-score = −2.5).
evidence: The results section provides comparison of sojourn time between different BMD levels.

claim: Once the initial fracture occurred, the difference in sojourn time between a person with low BMD and a person with normal BMD was not as much as in those who have not yet sustained a fracture, especially for men.
source: Once the initial fracture occurred, the difference in sojourn time between a person with low BMD and a person with normal BMD was not as much as in those who have not yet sustained a fracture, especially for men.
evidence: The results section states the diminished effect of BMD on sojourn time after fracture.

claim: For a woman aged 70 years, with a BMD T-score = −1.5 and BMI being 26.6 kg/m2, no history of fall, no prior fracture, no comorbidities, the probability of transition from no fracture to fracture (10.1%) was not much different from the risk of mortality (8.6%).
source: For a woman aged 70 years, with a BMD T-score = −1.5 and BMI being 26.6 kg/m2, no history of fall, no prior fracture, no comorbidities, the probability of transition from no fracture to fracture (10.1%) was not much different from the risk of mortality (8.6%).
evidence: The results section provides specific risk estimates for a typical woman.

claim: Once a fracture has occurred in a woman aged 70 years with typical risk profile, her risk of next fracture increased by almost 1.7-fold (16.5%), which was greater than the risk of mortality (10.4%).
source: However, once a fracture has occurred, her risk of next fracture increased by almost 1.7-fold (16.5%), which was greater than the risk of mortality (10.4%).
evidence: The results section provides specific risk estimates for a woman after fracture.

claim: For a man with a similar profile as a woman, the risk of an initial fracture (6.0%) was lower than the risk of mortality (15.3%).
source: For a man with a similar profile as a woman, the risk of an initial fracture (6.0%) was lower than the risk of mortality (15.3%).
evidence: The results section provides specific risk estimates for a typical man.

claim: If a man has sustained a fracture, then his risk of mortality is predicted to increase to 26.3%.
source: If the man has sustained a fracture, then his risk of mortality is predicted to increase to 26.3%.
evidence: The results section provides specific mortality risk estimate for a man after fracture.

claim: For both men and women, the risk of mortality was associated with a lower BMD T-score and advancing age.
source: For both men and women, the risk of mortality was associated with a lower BMD T-score and advancing age (Figure 3).
evidence: The results section and Figure 3 show associations between BMD, age, and mortality.

claim: The mortality risk increased with the increasing number of fractures; however, the increase was more pronounced in men than in women.
source: Importantly, the mortality risk increased with the increasing number of fractures; however, the increase was more pronounced in men than in women.
evidence: The results section states the relationship between number of fractures and mortality by gender.

claim: Less than 50% of men who sustained a refracture survived longer than 5 years.
source: Less than 50% of men who sustained a refracture survived longer than 5 years.
evidence: The results section provides survival data for men with refracture.

claim: The prediction model has good calibration as there was a close agreement between the observed and predicted incidence of fracture and mortality.
source: The prediction model has good calibration as there was a close agreement between the observed and predicted incidence of fracture and mortality (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The results section and supplementary figure show model calibration.

claim: This is the first investigation into the transition between fracture and fracture-associated events.
source: This is, to our knowledge, the first investigation into the transition between fracture and fracture-associated events.
evidence: The discussion section claims novelty of the study approach.

claim: Women have a higher risk of fracture than men.
source: However, for each event our findings were similar to those from previous studies, in that women have a higher risk of fracture than men (Johnell and Kanis, 2005) and once men sustain the first fracture, risk of the second fracture is similar to that in women (Center et al., 2007).
evidence: The discussion section cites previous studies supporting this finding.

claim: Once men sustain the first fracture, risk of the second fracture is similar to that in women.
source: However, for each event our findings were similar to those from previous studies, in that women have a higher risk of fracture than men (Johnell and Kanis, 2005) and once men sustain the first fracture, risk of the second fracture is similar to that in women (Center et al., 2007).
evidence: The discussion section cites previous studies supporting this finding.

claim: Risk of death, regardless of fracture status, is greater in men than in women.
source: Moreover, in contrast to risk of fracture, risk of death, regardless of fracture status, is greater in men than in women (Bliuc and Center, 2016; Kannegaard et al., 2010).
evidence: The discussion section cites previous studies supporting this finding.

claim: Adverse events related to surgery to repair a fractured hip have been implicated in the increased mortality observed among the older people.
source: Adverse events related to surgery to repair a fractured hip have been also implicated in the increased mortality observed among the older people (Nikkel et al., 2015).
evidence: The discussion section cites a study on surgical complications and mortality.

claim: The specific cause for long-term increase in mortality following hip fracture and other types of fracture is largely unknown.
source: However, the specific cause for long-term increase in mortality following hip fracture and other types of fracture is largely unknown.
evidence: The discussion section acknowledges a knowledge gap.

claim: The role of comorbidities in post-fracture mortality has been reported but with inconsistent findings across studies.
source: The role of comorbidities has been reported but with inconsistent findings across studies (Cenzer et al., 2016; Cree et al., 2000; Liem et al., 2013).
evidence: The discussion section cites studies showing inconsistent findings on comorbidities.

claim: Risk factors for fracture such as low bone mineral density, bone loss, and low muscle strength have recently been linked to mortality risk in the general population as well as post-fracture mortality.
source: Risk factors for fracture such as low bone mineral density, bone loss, and low muscle strength have recently been linked to mortality risk in the general population as well as post-fracture mortality (Nguyen et al., 2007c; Van Der Klift et al., 2002; Kado et al., 2000; Rantanen et al., 2000; Pham et al., 2017).
evidence: The discussion section cites multiple studies linking fracture risk factors to mortality.

claim: After an initial fracture, factors other than BMD might play a more important role than BMD in the progression to subsequent fractures and premature death.
source: This suggests that after an initial fracture, factors other than BMD might play a more important role than BMD in the progression to subsequent fractures and premature death.
evidence: The discussion section infers this from the sojourn time findings.

claim: Any intervention strategy which focuses on improving BMD would be more beneficial if implemented at early stage than at later stages.
source: The shorter transition time after an initial fracture also suggests that any intervention strategy which focuses on improving BMD would be more beneficial if implemented at early stage than at later stages.
evidence: The discussion section infers this clinical implication from the findings.

claim: All existing prediction models such as the Garvan Fracture Risk Calculator and FRAX provide only an estimate of fracture risk, with no estimate of mortality risk.
source: All existing prediction models such as the Garvan Fracture Risk Calculator (Nguyen et al., 2008) and FRAX (Kanis et al., 2008) provide only an estimate of fracture risk, with no estimate of mortality risk.
evidence: The discussion section identifies limitations of existing tools with citations.

claim: Mortality is clearly strongly associated with fracture.
source: This is a weakness because mortality is clearly strongly associated with fracture (Cree et al., 2000; Bliuc et al., 2009; Nguyen et al., 2007c) and treatment can reduce fracture-associated mortality risk (Lyles et al., 2007; Reid et al., 2018).
evidence: The discussion section cites studies supporting the fracture-mortality association.

claim: Treatment can reduce fracture-associated mortality risk.
source: This is a weakness because mortality is clearly strongly associated with fracture (Cree et al., 2000; Bliuc et al., 2009; Nguyen et al., 2007c) and treatment can reduce fracture-associated mortality risk (Lyles et al., 2007; Reid et al., 2018).
evidence: The discussion section cites studies showing treatment effects on mortality.

claim: Existing prediction models do not provide the benefit in terms of fracture reduction and increased survival if a high-risk patient opts for treatment.
source: Moreover, the risk estimate produced by these prediction models are not put into context. They do not provide the benefit in terms of fracture reduction and increased survival (and potential risk) if a high-risk patient opts for treatment; limiting the communication of risk and clinically useful discussions between patients and their physicians.
evidence: The discussion section identifies another limitation of existing tools.

claim: The lack of adverse events estimation in the existing fracture risk prediction tools can be an obstacle for both patients and doctors to be fully aware of the significance of the patients' bone health condition.
source: However, the lack of adverse events estimation in the existing fracture risk prediction tools can be an obstacle for both patients and doctors to be fully aware of the significance of the patients' bone health condition, which would lead to under-management of the conditions.
evidence: The discussion section infers this clinical implication.

claim: Patients do not always appreciate the serious consequence of fracture (e.g., subsequent fractures and mortality), and as a result, they usually underestimate their risk of adverse outcomes.
source: Patients do not always appreciate the serious consequence of fracture (e.g., subsequent fractures and mortality), and as a result, they usually underestimate their risk of adverse outcomes.
evidence: The discussion section states a clinical observation.

claim: Patients are concerned about quality of life and mortality, and providing the estimated risk of mortality can motivate them to take preventive measures.
source: Patients are however concerned about quality of life and mortality, and providing the estimated risk of mortality can motivate them to take preventive measures.
evidence: The discussion section infers this clinical implication.

claim: Skeletal age can be defined as the age of an individual's skeleton as a result of the individual's risk factors for fracture.
source: Based on the idea of 'lung age' (Morris and Temple, 1985) and 'effective age' (Spiegelhalter, 2016), skeletal age can be defined as the age of an individual's skeleton as a result of the individual's risk factors for fracture.
evidence: The discussion section defines skeletal age with citations to similar concepts.

claim: In the normal circumstance, skeletal age is the same as chronological age, but in high-risk individuals, skeletal age is greater than chronological age.
source: In the normal circumstance, skeletal age is the same as chronological age, but in high-risk individuals, skeletal age is greater than chronological age.
evidence: The discussion section explains the concept of skeletal age.

claim: For a 70-year-old man who has sustained a fracture, the hazard ratio of 1.67 is equivalent to a loss of approximately 5.4 years of life.
source: For instance, for a 70-year-old man who has sustained a fracture, the hazard ratio of 1.67 (Figure 2B) is equivalent to a loss of ~ 5.4 years of life (log(1.67)/log(1.1)).
evidence: The discussion section provides a specific calculation example with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: For an individual who has sustained a fracture, each standard deviation lower in femoral neck BMD on average takes around 1.5 years of life of the individual.
source: Moreover, for an individual who has sustained a fracture, each standard deviation lower in femoral neck BMD on average take around 1.5 years of life of the individual.
evidence: The discussion section provides a specific estimate of BMD effect on life years.

claim: In elderly hip fracture patients, intravenous zoledronic acid reduced the risk of subsequent fracture by 35% and reduced mortality risk by 28%, regardless of bone mineral density.
source: In a placebo-controlled trial, Lyles and colleagues found that among elderly hip fracture patients, intravenous zoledronic acid reduced the risk of subsequent fracture by 35% and reduced mortality risk by 28%, regardless of bone mineral density (Lyles et al., 2007).
evidence: The discussion section cites a specific clinical trial with treatment effects.

claim: In osteopenic patients with a fracture, zoledronic acid reduced mortality risk with an odds ratio of 0.65 (95% CI, 0.40–1.05).
source: A recent placebo-controlled trial further showed that in osteopenic patients with a fracture, zoledronic acid also reduced mortality risk with an odds ratio of 0.65 (95% CI, 0.40–1.05) (Reid et al., 2018).
evidence: The discussion section cites a clinical trial with specific effect size.

claim: Treatment of osteoporotic patients with medications with proven fracture efficacy reduced mortality risk by approximately 10%.
source: A review of all clinical trials reported that treatment of osteoporotic patients with medications with proven fracture efficacy reduced mortality risk by approximately 10% (Bolland et al., 2010).
evidence: The discussion section cites a review of clinical trials.

claim: A recent meta-analysis found that the effect of bisphosphonate treatment on mortality was less certain.
